introduction: Xenophon, Anabasis 5.8.1–12 and selected 5.8.13–26. 254 Greek words in 5 paragraphs.

Based on Anabasis 5.8.1–26. Xenophon narrates accusations against himself and his own defense. The condensed dialogue and general clauses are teaching adaptations; his explanation is presented as his claim, not an independently established verdict.

Read once for the argument, then translate paragraph by paragraph. Use the glosses during the first pass; translate the closing paragraph continuously. Submit your connected English translation using the reading submission box.

The vocabulary panel separates new required entries from review words. Paragraph glosses supply additional reading support; a gloss alone does not make a word or an advanced construction a production requirement.

paragraphs.greek: Οἱ στρατιῶται, ἐκ πολλῶν κινδύνων σωθέντες, οὐ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐπαύσαντο. ἔτι γὰρ περὶ μισθοῦ καὶ τροφῆς καὶ τῶν στρατηγῶν ἔργων διεφέροντο. ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τινὲς τὸν Ξενοφῶντα ᾐτιῶντο ὅτι ἄνδρας ἔπαισεν. ὁ δὲ οὐκ ἀπῆλθεν, ἀλλὰ λόγον δοῦναι ἤθελεν. ἐρωτᾷ οὖν τίς ἐστιν ὁ κατηγορῶν καὶ πότε ἔπαθεν ἃ λέγει.

Εἷς τῶν ἀνδρῶν ἀναστὰς λέγει ὅτι ὑπὸ τοῦ στρατηγοῦ ἐπλήγη. ὁ Ξενοφῶν ἐρωτᾷ διὰ τί. οὐ γὰρ ἀρκεῖ, φησίν, εἰπεῖν ὅτι ἔπαθές τι· δεῖ καὶ τὰ πρὸ τοῦ ἔργου δηλοῦν. οἱ δὲ παρόντες ἀκούουσιν ἀμφοτέρων. ἡ μὲν αἰτία χαλεπή ἐστιν, ἡ δὲ ἀπόκρισις οὐ πᾶσαν ἀπορίαν εὐθὺς λύει. δεῖ οὖν ἀκριβῶς ἐξετάζειν τὰ λεγόμενα.

Ὁ Ξενοφῶν τὴν πορείαν ἀναμιμνῄσκει τοὺς στρατιώτας. ἐν γὰρ τῷ χειμῶνι πολλοὶ ἔκαμνον, καὶ οἱ πολέμιοι ἐγγὺς ἦσαν. ὁ μένων ὄπισθεν ἐκινδύνευεν. ὁ στρατηγὸς οὖν φοβεῖται μὴ οἱ ἄνδρες ἀπόλωνται· δέδοικε δὲ μὴ οὐ βούλωνται ἀναστῆναι. ἔλεγεν ὅτι πρὸς σωτηρίαν ἐκέλευε βαδίζειν, οὐ πρὸς ἑαυτοῦ κέρδος.

paragraphs.greek: Ὅταν ὁ στρατιώτης κάμνῃ, βοηθείας δεῖται. ὃς ἂν τὸν ἑταῖρον καταλίπῃ, οὐ μόνον ἐκεῖνον ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ κοινὸν βλάπτει. ταῦτα ὁ στρατηγὸς λέγει, ἵνα οἱ ἀκούοντες τὴν χρείαν ἐξετάζωσιν. οὐ μέντοι πᾶν ἔργον δίκαιόν ἐστιν ὅτι ὁ ποιῶν χρήσιμον αὐτὸ νομίζει. ζητῶμεν οὖν καὶ τὸν τρόπον καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν.

Ἐν τῇ διηγήσει οἱ στρατιῶται τῶν παλαιῶν πόνων μνημονεύουσιν, καὶ ὁ Ξενοφῶν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γνώμην ἀπολογεῖται. ἡμεῖς δὲ δύο ἐρωτήσεις ποιούμεθα. τί φησιν ὁ κατήγορος, καὶ τί ἀποκρίνεται ὁ στρατηγός; ἔπειτα ἐρωτῶμεν τίς τὴν διήγησιν γράφει. ὁ γὰρ κρινόμενος καὶ ὁ γράφων ὁ αὐτός ἐστιν. τοῦτο οὔτε πάντα ψευδῆ ποιεῖ οὔτε πάντα ἀληθῆ ἀποδείκνυσιν.

reading.translation:
The soldiers, saved from many dangers, had not escaped all their troubles. They still disputed about pay, food, and the generals’ actions. In the assembly some accused Xenophon of striking men. He did not leave, but wished to give an account. He therefore asks who the accuser is and when he suffered what he alleges.

One of the men stands up and says that he was struck by the general. Xenophon asks why. For it is not enough, he says, to say that you suffered something; one must also make clear what preceded the act. Those present listen to both. The charge is serious, but the response does not immediately resolve every difficulty. One must therefore examine carefully what is said.

Xenophon reminds the soldiers of the march. In winter many were exhausted, and the enemy were nearby. Anyone remaining behind was in danger. The general therefore fears that the men may perish; he is afraid that they may be unwilling to get up. He said that he ordered them to march for their safety, not for his own gain.

Whenever a soldier is exhausted, he needs help. Whoever abandons his companion harms not only him but also the community. The general says these things so that the listeners may examine the need. Yet not every action is just because its doer considers it useful. Let us therefore investigate both the manner and the cause.

In the narrative the soldiers remember their former hardships, and Xenophon defends his own intention. We ask two questions: what does the accuser say, and what does the general reply? Then we ask who writes the account. For the man being judged and the writer are the same. This neither makes everything false nor proves everything true.

body: Read these related expressions in the lesson’s argument. κατηγορία means “accusation”; ἀπολογία means “defense”; μαρτυρία means “testimony”.
Explain which expression fits an action, a person, or an evaluation. A shared root connects meanings but does not make the words interchangeable in a sentence.

grammar.intro: II 22α–β. Original explanations and exercises follow the course grammar progression. Examples are teaching compositions, not additional ancient testimony. Complete each topic before the required grammar check.
objectives: Clauses of fearing, including μή and μή οὐ, with mood and sequence handled at the chapter’s level.
Indefinite and general clauses: recognize relative or temporal signals, ἄν where appropriate, and the force of the subjunctive.
Introduce the chapter’s indirect statements and indirect questions; preserve the original speaker, pronouns, and question word.
Compare a direct claim, a reported claim, and a fear. Gloss any secondary-sequence optatives retained in an original extract until Lesson 43.

sections.title: 1. Fear clauses: μή and μή οὐ
body: After a verb of fearing, μή introduces the feared event: φοβοῦμαι μὴ ἀπόληται, “I fear that he may perish.” It is not translated “I fear that he may not perish.” To fear that something will not happen, use μή οὐ: φοβοῦμαι μὴ οὐ ἔλθῃ, “I fear that he may not come.” Separate the clause introducer from the negation.

Primary sequence normally takes the subjunctive for a prospective event. After a historical main verb, an optative may appear, or the subjunctive may be retained. We support the optative in reading here and teach it fully in Lessons 42–43. Fear about a fact already treated as actual can use an indicative; do not force every fear into an imagined future.

sections.title: 2. Indefinite relatives and general time clauses
body: An indefinite relative clause can use ἄν with a subjunctive: ὃς ἂν βοηθῇ, “whoever helps.” A general temporal clause uses combinations such as ὅταν (ὅτε + ἄν), “whenever,” and ἐπειδάν, “whenever/when.” The construction envisages any occasion or person meeting the description, rather than identifying one completed event.

Relative pronouns still take their case from their role inside the clause. In ᾧ ἂν βοηθῇς, the dative is required by βοηθέω. Distinguish a definite temporal ὅτε with indicative from a general ὅταν with subjunctive. Past general conditions with optative will be treated systematically later.

sections.title: 3. A claim and a report of that claim
body: Direct speech gives a speaker’s words as an utterance. Indirect statement embeds their claim under a reporting verb. λέγει ὅτι ἐπλήγη means “He says that he was struck”: the passive aorist belongs to the claim, not to the act of reporting. Identifying the report does not certify its truth.

With ὅτι or ὡς, the embedded clause remains finite. An infinitive construction is also common after suitable verbs: φησὶ τὸν στρατηγὸν παίειν. Its expressed subject is accusative; the general, not the reporting speaker, strikes. We develop the governing-verb patterns and relative tense in Lesson 40.

table.title: 3. A claim and a report of that claim
rows: He says, “I was struck.” Direct speech.
He says that he was struck. Finite indirect statement.
He says that the general strikes. Accusative and infinitive.
He says that he did not strike. Negative embedded claim.
two common introductions to an indirect assertion

sections.title: 4. Reporting questions without losing the question
body: An indirect question preserves what is being asked: ἐρωτᾷ τίς ἔπαισεν, “He asks who struck.” A question word such as τίς, πῶς, or πότε does not become a relative merely because the question is embedded. A yes/no question can use εἰ, “whether.”

Track person and reference when shifting from direct speech. “Why did you strike me?” becomes “He asks why the general struck him.” The original “you” and “me” cannot both remain unchanged in a narrator’s report. At this stage use primary reporting frames; historical sequence is supported until formal instruction in Lesson 43.

table.title: 4. Reporting questions without losing the question
rows: He asks whether the general struck.
ἐρωτᾷ διὰ τί ὁ στρατηγὸς αὐτὸν ἔπαισεν.
He asks why the general struck him.
What should I do? → He asks what he should do.

summary.title: Grammar Summary
items: 1. Fear clauses: μή and μή οὐ: After a verb of fearing, μή introduces the feared event: φοβοῦμαι μὴ ἀπόληται, “I fear that he may perish.” It is not translated “I fear that he may not perish.” To fear that something will not happen, use μή οὐ: φοβοῦμαι μὴ οὐ ἔλθῃ, “I fear that he may not come.” Separate the clause introducer from the negation.

2. Indefinite relatives and general time clauses: An indefinite relative clause can use ἄν with a subjunctive: ὃς ἂν βοηθῇ, “whoever helps.” A general temporal clause uses combinations such as ὅταν (ὅτε + ἄν), “whenever,” and ἐπειδάν, “whenever/when.” The construction envisages any occasion or person meeting the description, rather than identifying one completed event.

3. A claim and a report of that claim: Direct speech gives a speaker’s words as an utterance. Indirect statement embeds their claim under a reporting verb. λέγει ὅτι ἐπλήγη means “He says that he was struck”: the passive aorist belongs to the claim, not to the act of reporting. Identifying the report does not certify its truth.

4. Reporting questions without losing the question: An indirect question preserves what is being asked: ἐρωτᾷ τίς ἔπαισεν, “He asks who struck.” A question word such as τίς, πῶς, or πότε does not become a relative merely because the question is embedded. A yes/no question can use εἰ, “whether.”

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Anabasis
body: This lesson returns to Book 5, after the sight of the sea, when accusations expose strains inside the army. The commander’s defense is also part of his self-presentation as author. Follow the complaint, the explanation, and the reaction separately. The question of how a group survives must remain connected with the question of how its members are treated.

The seven-book narrative begins with an expedition inland: in 401 BCE Cyrus the Younger challenges his brother, the Persian king Artaxerxes II. Cyrus dies at Cunaxa, leaving his Greek mercenaries in danger. After the loss of their senior commanders, the soldiers must reorganize, negotiate, find supplies, and fight their way toward the Black Sea. Xenophon emerges as one of their leaders.

The famous sight of the sea in Book 4 does not end the book—or solve every problem. Books 5–7 continue through disputes over leadership, dealings with Greek cities, and service in Thrace before the remaining troops join a Spartan commander. Survival is an extended political and logistical task. A triumphant moment can coexist with unpaid wages, competing interests, and an uncertain destination.

Reading invitation: begin Book 3, chapter 1, where Xenophon enters the leadership crisis, and compare his speeches with the practical decisions in Book 4, chapter 5. He is both participant and author, often describing himself in the third person. Ask what his narrative helps us see about leadership and how it presents his own reputation. The linked complete translation lets you follow the story beyond the celebrated mountain crossing.

links.title: Read the complete Anabasis — English translation

sections.title: The retreat does not end at the sea
body: The celebrated sight of the Black Sea occurs in Book 4 of the Anabasis, but the narrative continues through Book 7. Food, pay, service, and command remain contested. In Book 5, soldiers bring accusations concerning their leaders’ behavior. Survival has not removed the need to ask whether power was used justly.

The charge against Xenophon concerns striking men. He responds by asking about the circumstances and presenting acts of coercion as connected with the army’s needs. That explanation must be heard as a defense. It does not automatically prove that every act was necessary or proportionate.

sections.title: Participant and author
body: Xenophon is both a participant in the hearing and the author through whom we hear it. His narrative gives the commander’s reasoning and the soldiers’ reactions, but it is not an independent record from the accuser’s perspective. This does not make it useless or entirely false. It means that interpretation must account for the author’s position.

Separate four categories in your notes: accusation, response, supporting detail, and information still missing. A claim about intention belongs to the response unless other evidence supports it. An audience’s approval is evidence about reception; it does not substitute for examining the action.

sections.title: Evidence hearing
body: Assign one reader the accusation and another the defense. Each must summarize the other’s claim accurately before responding. A third reader identifies where the text reports fear, what event is feared, and whether the feared event is positive or negative. Confusing μή with μή οὐ can reverse the commander’s stated concern.

Translate the opening hearing with support, then translate the general clauses and final reflection as connected prose. End with a short account beginning “Xenophon says...” and a separate sentence beginning “The narrative leaves uncertain...”. Keep the two claims visibly distinct.

questions.prompt: Does seeing the sea end the Anabasis?
questions.answer: No; Books 5–7 continue the problems of return and service.

questions.prompt: Why examine Xenophon’s dual role?
questions.answer: He narrates a hearing in which he was the accused leader.

questions.prompt: What does audience approval establish most directly?
Where should a claimed intention first be categorized?
questions.answer: Under the speaker’s response, pending support.

questions.prompt: Analyze or translate: φοβοῦμαι μὴ ἔλθῃ.

choices.text: I fear that he may come.
choices.feedback: Correct. After a verb of fearing, μή introduces the feared event: φοβοῦμαι μὴ ἀπόληται, “I fear that he may perish.” It is not translated “I fear that he may not perish.” To fear that something will not happen, use μή οὐ: φοβοῦμαι μὴ οὐ ἔλθῃ, “I fear that he may not come.” Separate the clause introducer from the negation.
